test_cases.question: What are the health benefits of electrifying school buses?

expected_passages.text_snippet: Diesel exhaust—classified as a carcinogen by the World Health Organization—contains particulate matter, cancer-causing air toxins, nitrogen oxides, and volatile organic compounds. The pollution levels of school buses are closely tied to the age of the bus fleet. Past research has found that a 30-year-old diesel bus produces two to three times more onboard pollution than a three-year-old bus across similar time frames.

In addition to cancer, exposure to diesel exhaust can lead to increased asthma symptoms and a host of other respiratory illnesses and health impacts such as reduced lung function, more frequent asthma attacks, and impaired cognitive development. Children are especially susceptible to these risks due to their ongoing respiratory development, smaller average lung size, and increased activity levels.

synthesis_ground_truth.canonical_answer: Electrifying school buses eliminates exposure to diesel exhaust, which the WHO classifies as a carcinogen containing particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and volatile organic compounds. Children are especially vulnerable to these pollutants due to their developing respiratory systems, and exposure has been linked to increased asthma, reduced lung function, and impaired cognitive development. Older diesel buses produce two to three times more onboard pollution than newer models, making electrification particularly beneficial for fleets with aging vehicles.
key_facts: diesel exhaust classified as carcinogen by WHO
children especially susceptible due to developing respiratory systems
older diesel buses produce 2-3x more pollution than newer buses
exposure linked to asthma, reduced lung function, impaired cognitive development

test_cases.question: How does land value capture support transit-oriented development?

expected_passages.text_snippet: Land value capture (LVC) is a public financing strategy that can recover a portion of the real estate value that development along the metro corridor generates for private landowners. Deployed effectively, LVC can help fund the growth of mass transit and allied infrastructure.

Portland (United States) is a notable case. The city strategically invests and offers incentives that foster PPPs to help overcome market barriers. Over the two decades since its inception, the TOD program has invested over $46 million cumulatively. As a result, the 41 TOD projects completed at the time of this writing have leveraged $15.3 million of this investment to support development activities worth more than $684 million

synthesis_ground_truth.canonical_answer: Land value capture (LVC) is a public financing strategy that recovers a portion of the real estate value generated by transit corridor development for private landowners, redirecting it to fund mass transit and allied infrastructure. When synergized with transit-oriented development, LVC creates a virtuous cycle: transit investment raises land values, which can be partially captured to fund further transit expansion and local area improvements. Portland's TOD program demonstrates this effectively, having invested $46 million over two decades to leverage over $684 million in development activities.
key_facts: LVC recovers real estate value generated by transit corridor development
LVC revenue can fund mass transit growth and allied infrastructure
Portland TOD program invested $46 million and leveraged $684 million in development
synergizing LVC and TOD creates a virtuous cycle of value creation and capture
